notes.title: 우리 means "my" too
notes.text: Koreans say 우리 (our) for family, home and country even when English says "my": 우리 엄마 (my mom), 우리 집 (my home). It sounds warmer and more natural than 제 엄마.

notes.title: Family words for friends
notes.text: Koreans also use family words for people who aren't related: Ji-woo calls Min-jun 형, and you can call an older woman like Grandma 할머니. Calling an older person by just their name sounds rude, so a title is safer.

And Grandma is the boss of the boarding house!
That's right, I'm the owner!

No. I'm a student at a university language school.

notes.title: Titles at work
notes.text: Koreans often call people by job titles instead of names: 사장님 (boss), 선생님 (teacher, and also doctors), 기사님 (driver). Adding 님 makes a title polite.

notes.title: Country + 사람
notes.text: To say a nationality, add 사람 (person) to the country: 한국 사람, 미국 사람, 일본 사람. For a language, add 어 or 말: 한국어 / 한국말, 일본어. English is the exception: 영어.

notes.title: Unlucky four
notes.text: 사 (four) sounds like 사 (死, death), so many Korean buildings skip the fourth floor or write it as "F" in elevators. In phone numbers, zero is said 공.

notes.title: Self-introduction (자기소개)
notes.text: In Korean classes, new jobs and clubs, people give a short 자기소개: name, country, job or school, and family. Finish with 잘 부탁드립니다 ("I'm in your care"), which you'll hear everywhere.
